Executive Summary
This United Nations Development Assistance Framework (UNDAF) has been prepared in response to the UN Secretary General’s reform proposals. It aims at strategically directing UN system’s development assistance in Uganda to the country’s development priorities and goals in the 2001-2005 period. The preparation of UNDAF and the preceding Common Country Assessment (CCA) promoted collaboration among the United Nations system agencies in Uganda, thus furthering the vision of a more coherent and better co-ordinated UN development and humanitarian assistance programmes in Uganda.
Uganda's UNDAF addresses key issues previously analysed in the CCA. Four UNDAF goals and related objectives have been developed to address these issues. These goals and objectives derive from Uganda’s over-arching goal of reducing the proportion of people below the poverty line to less than 10% by 2017, as is enshrined in the country’s Poverty Eradication Action Plan (PEAP). However, the United Nations Country Team (UNCT) also considered other essential crosscutting issues notably human rights, HIV/AIDS, environment and gender.  These will be mainstreamed in pursuit of the four UNDAF goals, which are:
 To contribute to sustainable, broad-based and equitable economic growth and social transformation
To contribute to enhanced observation of human rights and promotion of good governance, gender equality and security
To contribute to sustainable interventions for empowering the poor to raise their incomes
To contribute to enhanced quality of life of Ugandan population (women, men, girls and boys) with a particular focus on the poor and vulnerable groups
A number of objectives are specified under each one of these goals. Building on the UN system’s unique characteristics relating to neutrality and mandate for a rights-based approach to promoting sustainable development and peace, the UNCT opted for six strategic entry-points in pursuit of the UNDAF objectives. These are: technical advice and assistance in policy formulation and/or reform; capacity building; advocacy and social mobilisation; provision and dissemination of information for policy change; provision of services; and catalytic actions to stimulate large-scale implementation, which include assistance in the elaboration of guidelines and support to pilot/demonstration projects.
Annex 1 contains a matrix indicating outputs, indicators and collaborating agencies for the various UNDAF strategic areas. The information in the annex will guide the implementation, monitoring and evaluation of the UNDAF.  The Country Team is committed to promoting government ownership and leadership of the development process. It will use inter-agency collaboration to achieve the UNDAF goals and to optimize on the use of available resources. Potentials for synergy will be seized and the participation of government, civil society and other development agencies will be encouraged. The UN Country Team will work towards enhanced resource mobilisation to meet the UNDAF goals. It commits itself to ensuring the most cost-effective utilisation of such resources so that the greatest impact is made on targeted beneficiaries.
I.	Rationale
A.	Background	
The dawn of the new millennium provides the UN family in Uganda with an opportunity to maximise the scope for collaboration between the people of Uganda, the UN system as well as the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank (WB) – the Bretton Woods institutions - drawing upon the UN Agencies’ particular mandates and areas of comparative advantage. Recent developments in the UN, that reflect the implementation of the Secretary-General’s reform agenda, provide new opportunities for enhancing the visibility and impact of UN system cooperation on the development and well-being of the people in member countries.  
In March 1997, Mr Kofi Annan, the UN Secretary-General, submitted to the President of the General Assembly reform proposals of the United Nations system, urging for the attainment of the following at the country level:
Cooperation - stronger unity of purpose and collaboration through a mix of parallel and joint programming among UN agencies and between the UN system, its member states and other development partners;
Coordination - improved goal - oriented collaboration, coherence and mutual reinforcement in achieving the objectives set at the UN conferences, conventions and declarations;
Capacity - to effectively and efficiently implement the UN’s development mandate (more efficient use of limited resources, based on improved division of labour, rationalisation of resource allocation and streamlining of procedures); and 
Clarification - secured role of the UN system in development cooperation with countries, taking into account the UN system's comparative advantage by using its unique strengths as a development partner.
These proposals were endorsed by the UN General Assembly in resolution A/53/192 and were confirmed by the UN Administrative Committee on Coordination in the “Statement and Guidance Note on implementation of Common Country Assessment (CCA) and United Nations Development Assistance Framework (UNDAF)”. The CCA provides an assessment and analysis of the development situation of a country. The UNDAF, on the other hand, is a strategic document that articulates mechanisms for strengthening collaboration within the UN system and with government and other partners in pursuit of the country’s development priorities and goals.
UNDAF preparation process in Uganda
The UN reform process and Uganda’s openness to views expressed by its development partners enhanced the preparation of this UNDAF. The process was in two phases, namely, the identification of issues on which to base the UNDAF; and the actual formulation of the document. 
i) Preparatory phase
The Country Team recognises that drafting the UNDAF is a learning process that will enhance the UN system’s joint programming and operational linkages.  The challenge for the first UNDAF is, therefore, to move from a position of individual agency programming and operation and work towards collaboration and joint programming, monitoring and evaluation.  Consequently, in November 2000, the UN Resident Co-ordinator (UNRC), in consultation with members of the UNCT, charged a team of senior programme managers from the various UN agencies and Bretton Woods’s institutions (BWIs) with the responsibility of managing the UNDAF process. This team was designated as the UNDAF Steering Committee and was initially chaired by UNFPA and subsequently by UNDP. The list of members of this committee appears in Annex 6.
The Steering Committee developed the ToR and work plan for the UNDAF process. A milestone in the process was the joint UNDAF workshop that involved representatives of government and members of the UNDAF Steering Committee. The aim of the workshop was to discuss the main issues on which the UNDAF should concentrate. The challenges mentioned in the CCA, the thrust of the PEAP, other critical issues such as human rights, equity (gender and region), environment and the comparative advantage of the UN system agencies were used to determine the issues to focus on. This set of issues was shared with UNCT for ratification.
Building on the commonly agreed set of issues, the Steering Committee defined UNDAF goals and accordingly constituted five working groups composed of staff from the various UN agencies. The areas of focus covered the following concerns: Group 1 - Rapid and sustainable economic growth and structural transformation; Group 2 - Good governance and security; Group 3 - Increased ability of the poor to raise their incomes; and Group 4 - Enhanced quality of life of the poor. A fifth group was set up to analyse issues relating to ‘’protection and support to vulnerable groups’’.  
These groups drafted the various sections of the UNDAF document. Each working group was led by the UN agency whose comparative advantage accorded with the set of issues assigned to the group. The Terms of Reference developed by the Steering Committee on the basis of the generic ones and the UNDAF guidelines from UNDG guided the working groups. This first phase was backstopped by a National Consultant and covered the months of November and December 2000. 
ii) The formulation phase
Between January and March 2001, the various working groups assisted by a National Consultant, embarked on the substantive formulation of the UNDAF, using a framework that had been developed by the Steering Committee and approved by the UNCT. The working groups went through several iterations in developing the draft. At the UNDAF Working Group Retreat (22 February), the initial drafts from the various working groups were reviewed and the comments and suggestions made during the retreat enabled the groups to become more focused. It was also agreed that the protection and support of vulnerable groups be considered as crosscutting issues. Subsequently, each working group used short work sessions to produce another draft that clearly linked the UNDAF goals, objectives, and strategic areas of support, expected outputs, indicators, and collaborating members of the UNCT. This advanced draft was reviewed by the Steering Committee whose comments shaped the quality of the draft that was shared with the UNCT. Comments on this draft were duly reflected in the revised version that was shared with government, which endorsed the proposed UNDAF strategic direction and areas of support. Comments from members of the CCA/UNDAF Learning Network were integrated in this penultimate version, which was edited before printing.   
C.	Comparative advantage of the UN system 
The UN is a unique organisation that derives its mandate from a broad consensus amongst its member states. This consensus is reflected in a series of conventions and declarations. The unique characteristics of the UN system are: universality and impartiality; advocacy for people-centred and rights-based development policies and strategies; presentation and adherence to international standards and practices, greater social equity; capacity to play a facilitating role between internal and external parties; support to peace and security; and access to universal and regional databanks. 
Using these unique characteristics, the UN agencies and Bretton Woods institutions have indeed enabled Uganda to make important achievements on economic, social and political fronts after a long period of turmoil. The UN system advocates that policies being pursued should be in harmony with the international norms set in various conventions and treaties as well as the compacts made during the various UN conferences (Annex 2). Since 1986, Uganda has ratified a number of conventions (Annex 2). The cumulative effect of these initiatives has been a policy and legislative environment that is favourable to the pursuit of sustainable development and the promotion of social equity.
With support from UN agencies during the 1990s, legislative and policy measures, which embody principles, ideals and specific elements drawn from UN conventions, conferences and other international treaties, have been in force. 
The UN system was a key partner with the Government of Uganda, development partners and civil society in the formulation and revision of the PEAP as well as the formulation of sector-wide policies and plans for health, education and agriculture. The UN’s neutrality has enhanced its leadership role in advocating democratic governance, the holding of regular elections and the observance and protection of human rights. Indeed at the 2000 and 2001 CG meetings in the country, the UNRC presented statements on governance and on poverty, respectively, on behalf of the development assistance community. 
The UN system also has built partnerships with cultural, religious and political leaders, as well as Civil Society Organisations (CSOs) and Community Based Organisations (CBOs) in addressing other human development–related issues such human rights, promotion of gender equity and children’s rights and the control of HIV/AIDS.  In 2001, the UN system, through the UNDP, facilitated civil society organizations in preparing and presenting a joint response to government’s Poverty Status Report. The UNCT intends to maintain and strengthen this partnership in pursuit of UNDAF goals and objectives.
II.	 UNDAF goals and objectives 
A) Overview
The over-arching goal, which the UN system in Uganda will concentrate its activities over the 2001-2005 period, is to contribute to the well-being of Uganda’s population by supporting Uganda’s poverty eradication initiatives. Uganda’s strategic focus on reducing the proportion of people below the poverty line to less than 10% by 2017 is consistent with the international goals set at the World Summit for Social Development and the target date of 2015 when countries are expected to have reduced the proportion of those living in poverty by 50%. The country’s participatory development stance is consonant with the UN “Declaration on the Right to Development” which recognises the centrality of human beings as active participants in, and beneficiaries of development.  
In defining the UNDAF goals, the UN system relied on its CCA and the PEAP.  The four PEAP goals are i) Rapid and sustainable economic growth and structural transformation; ii) Good governance and security; iii) Increased ability of the poor to raise their incomes; and iv) Enhanced quality of life of the poor. 
Building on the UN global mandate, the CCA analysis and the PEAP’s strategic direction, the UNCT has identified the following priority cross-cutting issues for UNDAF: broad-based equitable growth and social justice, human rights, regional security, gender, environment and HIV/AIDS. Fundamentally, the UNDAF goals for 2001-2005 period are to contribute to:  
rapid, sustainable, broad-based and equitable economic growth and social transformation;
enhanced observation of human rights, and promotion of good governance and security; 
sustainable interventions for increasing the ability of the poor to raise their incomes; and
improved quality of life of the Ugandan population especially the poor and vulnerable groups.
In line with these UNDAF goals, the following objectives will be pursued. 
B) UNDAF Goals and related Objectives
UNDAF Goal 1. To contribute to sustainable, broad-based and equitable economic growth and social transformation
Government has continued to honour its commitments to the people of Uganda by providing an enabling environment for poverty reduction, the first goal of the Poverty Eradication Action Plan (PEAP). Economic growth and structural transformation requires a framework within which the private sector can expand. The main elements of this framework are (a) macro-economic stability; (b) equitable and efficient collection and use public resources for poverty reducing activities; and (c) the removal of constraints to private sector development. Government has prepared a comprehensive Medium-Term Competitiveness Strategy for the private sector, focusing on infrastructure provision, financial sector reforms, commercial justice sector and export promotion. Employment generation, adequate remuneration of the poor and export promotion are expected to enable the earning of more resources to finance government programmes in the area of service delivery.  
The opportunities to contribute to a rational, transparent, people-centred and sustainable development and poverty eradication are evident.  Poverty eradication depends on sustained high rates of economic growth, which in the case of Uganda requires the consolidation of ongoing economic reforms, increased investment in human resources, organisational development, strengthening the country’s position in the global economy, promotion of competitiveness and development of the private sector, and investment in the physical infrastructure and productive capacity with sound environmental management. 
Government and the UN, however, have recognised the inability of certain groups in society to benefit from the growth process. The UN system feels that while safety nets should be provided, the long-term goal of distributive justice should not be overlooked.  The UNCT is willing to support government in efforts in monitoring and counteracting adverse effects of any social dislocations arising from the growth process. The UNCT also recognises the effects of structural barriers and certain attitudes and values that marginalize the girl-child, increase women’s workload and prevent them from participating in, and benefiting from, the growth process.  Unless the structural barriers are removed and negative attitudes are changed, self-reliant and equitable development and the fight against HIV/AIDS could be impaired.
 While the Bretton Woods Institutions have a comparative advantage in providing credit for basic infrastructure and financial sector development, the UN system agencies have a comparative advantage in supporting catalytic actions that improve social service delivery and protect human rights. These agencies are also well positioned to advocate equitable and sustainable development so that the hitherto underprivileged groups and areas would progressively reap the benefits of economic growth. The UN system in Uganda is therefore convinced that macroeconomic development must go hand in hand with social transformation, with particular attention to equitable distribution of the benefits of growth, by paying particular attention to the rights and needs of the under privileged groups, human rights–based approach to development and environmental sustainability. 
The UN Country Team has identified the following objectives to support this goal: (1) To contribute to the promotion of macro-economic stability and economic growth and (2) To ensure broad-based, equitable and environmentally sound growth process.   Sound macro-economic policies, responsive sector programmes, effective public sector management, and proactive participation of the wider society in the process of development would buttress these objectives. The pursuit of these objectives will complement those being pursued by the Bretton Woods Institutions and the bilateral donors in form of budget support. UN system will advocate social justice and fair allocation of resources to the underprivileged, marginalised and poorest areas.  It will promote research on the link between economic growth and social transformation and on the impact of rapid economic growth on environment and household economy. It will also emphasise the need to promote qualitative assessment and monitoring of poverty. It will give special attention to analysing and responding to gender disparities and addressing the impact of HIV/AIDS on human development of especially the poor and the groups at most risk.  
UNDAF Goal 2.	To contribute to enhanced observation of human rights and promotion of good governance, gender equity and security
Uganda has had a chequered governance record since Independence in 1962. Good governance, which is a prerequisite for sustainable development, had eluded the country for long. However, more recent efforts in nurturing constitutional and democratic governance seem promising. Without good governance and security, it would become increasingly difficult to improve the incomes of the poor and hence their quality of life. While many areas of Uganda enjoy peace and development, quite a number of areas continue to be affected by armed conflict and other forms of insecurity, although the magnitude of the problem has somewhat lessened over the past two years. 
The effective enforcement of law and order, zero tolerance for corruption and the enforcement of transparency and accountability, if achieved, are likely to attract private sector investments, which in turn would provide employment opportunities, thereby contributing to poverty reduction. Without this the national Medium-Term Private Sector Competitiveness Strategy may not produce the expected results.
Civil and political rights have to be promoted simultaneously with economic, social and political rights. On the whole, poor people and other marginalized groups such as women; children and the elderly are more vulnerable to having their rights violated. In particular their social and economic rights such as the right to health, education, shelter and an adequate standard of living have not been realized. Social justice, the rights-based approach to development, underpinned by transparency and accountability are among the fundamental principles that Uganda is striving to adhere to as it pursues its commitments and compacts under various UN conventions and conferences. The UN, therefore, intends to support government efforts in promoting the protection of human rights, peace building, democratic governance through support to decentralization and the enhancement of service delivery as envisaged in the Sector-Wide Approaches.
National and regional conflicts can undermine the developmental gains made so far. The UN System in Uganda therefore intends to help government and civil society in promoting effective conflict resolution mechanisms, while engaging itself actively in peace building and democratisation.
In contributing to the pursuit of good governance and security, the UN system will focus on three objectives, namely, i) To contribute to strengthening the capacity of government and communities to protect human rights, maintain law and order, and ensure transparency and accountability at all levels; ii) To contribute to reduction of intra-country regional and gender disparities and other forms of exclusion, discrimination and marginalization at all levels of society through appropriate programmes; and iii) To contribute to ensuring national and regional (inter-country) security of individuals and communities. These objectives are consistent with the strategic actions under two of the objectives of the National Programme for Good Governance in the context of the Poverty Eradication Action Plan (PEAP); namely, (a) “Respect, Protection and Promotion of Human Rights and Equity;” and  (b) “Security, Peace Building and Conflict Resolution.” They will also be reinforced by long-term civic education and promotion of human rights.
The achievement of these objectives coupled with enhanced education and participation of the poor, especially women, will raise the status of the poor, thereby enabling them to be fully involved in promoting transparency and accountability, combating corruption, rallying for peace and security and protecting human rights nationally and regionally.  
UNDAF Goal 3.	To contribute to sustainable interventions for empowering the poor, especially women, to raise their incomes
The sustained economic growth has resulted into improvements in the economic levels of some Ugandans. While economic growth has been reasonably broad-based and has reduced the overall proportion of the population in poverty substantially, that effect has been uneven among different groups of the poor. Broadly, the population in the North has gotten poorer because of the persistent insecurity. Data from the 2001 Uganda Poverty Status Report indicates that poverty continues to be regionally concentrated, with the North and the East, respectively having the largest proportion of the poor. Moreover, the poverty gap and depth of poverty have increased in rural areas of the North and among women generally. Sector-wise, the major focus needs to be on improving the productivity and incomes of the non-crop farmers who benefited least.
Sustained high rates of economic growth and progress towards the eradication of absolute poverty and HIV/AIDS in Uganda require the participation of the poor. In order for this to happen, the poor need, among other things, to fully participate in the identification and definition of priority actions and to gain access to basic services, education and information. The Uganda Participatory Project/Process (UPPAP), in which the UNCT continues to be engaged, is partly helping to meet this need. Skills development and entrepreneurship training are among the support services that may promote social and economic empowerment of the poor, while behavioural change would lead to reduction in HIV/AIDS infection rates.  
Increased ability of the poor to raise their incomes requires, among other things, access to services, information, skills and appropriate technologies. Given that the majority of the poor derive their livelihoods from agriculture, the pursuit of this goal will be compliant with the goals of the 2000 Plan for Modernisation of Agriculture (PMA). Fostering a conducive environment for the performance of small and micro-finance institutions would also contribute to the economic empowerment of the poor. This would be consistent with the Medium Term Competitiveness Strategy for the private sector. The UNCT, however, advocates engagement in productive activities that do not degrade the natural resource base or unduly pollute the environment. In pursuit of UNDAF goal 3, the UN system seeks to attain two objectives. These are: i) To contribute to efforts aimed at improving agricultural productivity, food security and agricultural produce marketing infrastructure; and ii) To strengthen rural service delivery and outreach. 
UNDAF Goal 4.	To contribute to enhanced quality of life of Ugandan population (men, women, boys and girls) with a focus on the poor and vulnerable groups
Improving the quality of life and enhancing the human capital of the poor comprise an essential component of Uganda’s poverty eradication strategy. Policy goals, such as improving the health of the population, reducing infant and child mortality, raising the levels of educational attainment, providing safe and accessible drinking water, and sustaining the gains made in the fight against HIV/AIDS, are all important social welfare objectives in their own rights. They also play a vital role in enhancing the incomes of the poor. Uganda’s National Health Policy was approved in 1999 and its Health Sector Strategic Plan was launched in 2000. The plan’s priority actions include the delivery of a minimum quality of health care package nationwide, and strengthening of the health care delivery system and the legal and regulatory framework.  Special attention is being placed on increasing effective access for the poor, the difficult to reach and the otherwise disadvantaged with a view to reducing inequalities between various segments of the population. 
 Education is a key component of Uganda’s poverty eradication strategy. Better-educated mothers have healthier children, and education helps farmers to become more productive. Education is also a means of empowering the poor population – especially girls in poor households.  The Education Sector Investment Plan aims at ensuring equity of access to all levels of education; with specific emphasis on regional and gender imbalances; and on special education needs of children. 
The process of formulating social sector policies has brought together the UN system, government and civil society. The overall objective of the UN system is to encourage equitable provision of quality basic education and health care services with a particular focus on the poor and vulnerable groups (especially the elderly, women and children). Adherence to the principles of transparency and accountability in the delivery and management of these basic social services will be promoted by the UN system. 
In the health sector, for instance, the UN system intends to support quality service delivery and to promote mechanisms that enable communities to find and apply sustainable solutions for service delivery. The UNCT acknowledges the importance of having health facilities at community-level that deliver integrated curative, preventive and promotive health activities, and referral facilities that ensure continuity of care from the community-based facilities, while taking into account financial and other accessibility issues.  In education, there is a strong need to improve the quality of Universal Primary Education through the provision of necessary infrastructure and well-trained teachers. Access to and full completion of primary education by the girl child will be supported by the UN system. Similarly, in the water and sanitation sector, the UN system will support efforts to make safe water available to all, and to promote healthy behaviour throughout society. 
In light of the above considerations, the UN system will contribute to the following objectives i) To advocate the establishment of, and adherence to, acceptable standards in delivering services, ii) To promote equal access to and utilisation of basic social services; iii) To assist in the provision of quality health, education and safe water services; iv) To facilitate the integration of rights of vulnerable groups into health, education and water sector policy formulation and implementation; and v) To promote mechanisms that lead to self-reliance and durable solutions in health, education, water and sanitation sectors. The attainment of these objectives would complement the outcomes of the Education Sector Investment Plan and of the Health Sector Strategic Plan. 
III.	Strategic Entry-points and Areas of Intervention
For each objective, the UNCT identified, a number of strategic areas and grouped them according to strategic entry-points that will guide the implementation of the UNDAF and the review of UN agencies’ programmes that came into effect before the launching of this UNDAF. The following strategic entry-points were identified. 
Technical advice and assistance (TA) in policy formulation and/or reform
Capacity building (which is understood here both in human resources and in the establishment of infrastructure and equipment)
Advocacy and social mobilisation
Provision and dissemination of information for policy change
Provision of services
Catalytic action which includes (1) assistance in the elaboration of guidelines, and (2) the development of pilot projects/models to ensure large-scale implementation
The UNDAF goal and the corresponding objectives, strategic entry-points, and the composition of collaborating UN agencies appear in Annex1. Lead agencies will be identified to take charge of leveraging the strategic entry-point to enable the UNCT fulfil the UNDAF objectives. The co-operation strategies and modalities will in many cases involve the entire UN system while in other cases only those agencies working in a common area will be involved.
Objective 1 of UNDAF GOAL 1.  To contribute to macro-economic stability and economic growth.
With the support of BWIs, Uganda has restored macroeconomic stability. The economy has registered a GDP growth rate averaging 6% per annum in the last decade and inflation has been reduced to a single digit figure. Crucially, the country now has a comprehensive policy framework for eradicating poverty. The UN System affirms that the maintenance of macroeconomic stability and the achievement of sustained high rates of economic growth are necessary conditions for eradication of mass poverty. The UNCT however believes that appropriate actions should be taken by Government and its development partners to ensure the sustainability of the macro-economic stability. Insecurity problems continue to impact negatively on human development and the image of Uganda abroad.  Ensuring the rights of war-affected communities to basic social services is a high concern in many parts of northern and western Uganda and in some of the neighbouring countries. Besides having to disproportionately shoulder the burden of caring for children in the event of conflict, women are often targets of human rights abuse in situations of conflict. IV.	Implementation, Follow-up and Review Mechanisms
Implementation mechanisms
UNDAF is coming at a time when the 2001-2005 co-operation frameworks of some of the agencies (UNICEF, WFP, UNFPA and UNDP) have been approved. Other UN agencies such as FAO and UNHCR operate shorter planning cycles. This UNDAF therefore takes due cognisance of agreements already reached with GoU in this regard.  However, to the extent that these frameworks and related programmes are based on the PEAP and the CCA; from which this UNDAF took its cue, the strategic direction charted here would be consistent with those programmes. It is however expected that such programmes would be appropriately reoriented during annual reviews. New programmes will be expected to take their cues from the UNDAF and benefit from existing mechanisms for joint review and appraisal.
Besides informing programming, the UNDAF will be a basis for policy dialogue with government and other development partners, especially in contributing to the revision of the PEAP, the PRSP, the PMA, the formulation of additional sector plans and the UN engagement in the working groups handling Medium-Term Expenditure Frameworks (MTEF). It will also serve as an advocacy tool, particularly in promoting the rights-based approach and in safeguarding the interests and satisfying needs of disadvantaged areas and groups. As a tool for enhancing coherence and co-ordination of UN developmental and humanitarian activities, the UNDAF will provide a framework for resource mobilisation to support the transition from relief to development in parts of northern and western Uganda affected by civil strife. In this regard, the CAP will be harmonized with the UNDAF to enable it serve as an additional resource mobilisation instrument for the UNCT.
In order to achieve each of the stated UNDAF goals, one appropriate agency will take the lead in developing a co-ordinated inter-agency operational work-plan and implementation mechanisms through a participatory process involving all collaborating agencies mentioned in the matrix (Annex 1). The ultimate objective is to organise discussion on the UN system support to Uganda on coordinated thematic basis. Geographic and thematic concentration will be encouraged to promote impact and documentation of best practices and the benefits of using the UNDAF. Joint programming and creative ways of promoting a rights-based approach to development and mainstreaming of human development-related issues such as gender; HIV/AIDS and environment will be pursued. Synchronisation of the programming cycles of additional UN agencies and the rationalisation of operational procedures will enhance collaboration and clear the path to joint programming.
B) Monitoring and evaluation
The UNCT will develop an appropriate monitoring and evaluation framework, building on the indicators in Annex 1. In doing so, the UNTC will take into account existing monitoring and evaluation mechanisms of government and other development partners. The monitoring mechanisms will also draw upon databases that exist within government and the UN system. The lead agency will initiate a joint evaluation of the designated UNDAF goal in partnership with government and civil society.  Both Government and the UN are committed to Results-Oriented Management (ROM). This approach to development management will underpin the UNDAF monitoring and evaluation frameworks, especially the use of indicators to monitor progress towards the UNDAF goals and to evaluate the attainment of the expected UNDAF results. 
Availability of funds permitting, it is envisaged that periodic independent monitoring and an external evaluation would be a main feature of UNDAF implementation. The monitoring exercise would help to ascertain the relevance and validity of the strategic direction of the UNDAF to Uganda’s development priorities and goals. 
 The UNCT will ensure proper implementation through effective participation and co-ordination at appropriate technical levels. It will receive and analyse monitoring and evaluation reports and ensure that the recommendations and lessons learnt are incorporated in the UNDAF process. 
C) Partnership building
The formulation of the CCA and UNDAF has consolidated the partnerships among UN system agencies and with government, civil society as well as other development agencies. The UNCT will build on this achievement to enhance the position of the UN as a trusted development partner. Partnership building with other development agencies is also driven by the common desire to support Government in meeting its noble goal of reducing absolute poverty to less than 10% by 2017. In the specific case of civil society, the partnership will go beyond working with NGOs and CBOs as implementing partners to include enhancing their vibrancy in influencing public policy, monitoring poverty and the enforcing transparency and accountability. Capacity building support will be provided to meet this need. The bottom line here is the promotion of broader national ownership of development programmes and facilitating a more co-ordinated approach to the delivery of development assistance.
D) Co-ordination
Government plays a lead role in aid co-ordination through the Ministry of Finance, Planning, and Economic Development (MFPED). The CG process led by the World Bank and the Resident Co-ordinator system led by the UNDP complement this. Within the UN system, theme groups such as UNAIDS have been used to ensure a more co-ordinated delivery of development assistance in tackling specific problems. This same mechanism will be used to ensure a more co-ordinated implementation of the UNDAF, drawing upon work of the various donor-subgroups, for instance on social services and gender. The UN agencies are members of various donor-subgroups responsible for fostering harmonised donor support to various sector programmes. The potential tensions between decentralised planning and the sector-wide approach will be a subject of co-ordinated discussion to which the UNCT would participate. The results of such discussions will feed into the UNDAF implementation process. The sub-groups will also be vehicles for promoting the UNDAF objectives and ensuring that they remain relevant to Uganda’s development needs and priorities as partly reflected in the sector programmes. A major strength of this UNDAF is that it will enable the UN system and the Bretton Woods institutions to demonstrate to government and other development partners the value of operating in a more coherent and co-ordinated manner. 
V)	Programme Resources Framework
UN system collaboration and expeditious implementation of the UNDAF may enhance resource mobilisation, especially of non-core programme funding, particularly now that core resources are declining. The UN agencies are expected to collaborate in ensuring that resources are mobilised, pooled in a complementary and integrated manner and cost effectively targeted at priority areas for maximum impact.
An initial implementation activity for this UNDAF will be a resource mapping, which will clearly indicate the extent to which some of the UNDAF outputs can be realized using the available programme funds and the resource gap for which the UNCT shall produce and execute a resource mobilization strategy to access extra-budgetary resources.
